blocks.content: These two are easy to mix up by name alone, but they operate at completely different times: RUN executes during the build, CMD executes when a container starts.

RUN executes once, permanently, while the image is being assembled, its result becomes a layer baked into the image. CMD does not run at all during the build, it only defines what happens the moment a container is later started from that finished image.

blocks.alt: One shapes the image, the other shapes what happens when it runs

blocks.content: A Dockerfile can, and often does, have many RUN instructions, installing packages, creating directories, compiling code, each its own build step. CMD, by contrast, is effectively single: if you declare it multiple times, only the last one takes effect.

blocks.alt: Many RUN instructions are normal, only the last CMD matters

blocks.content:
FROM node:18
RUN apt-get update
RUN npm install -g pm2
RUN mkdir -p /app/logs
# ... many RUN lines are completely normal
CMD ["node", "index.js"]
# only one CMD actually takes effect

blocks.content: 3. What Each One Is Really For
blocks.text: 3. What Each One Is Really For

blocks.content: Think of it this way: RUN shapes what ends up inside the image, packages, files, compiled artifacts. CMD shapes what happens when that finished image is actually run, the process that becomes the container's reason for existing.

blocks.alt: Shaping the image versus shaping its runtime behavior

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: RUN executes during the build and can appear many times, CMD executes at container start and only the last one has any effect.
RUN builds the image's contents, CMD defines what a container started from that image actually does.
